title: JavaScript Fundamentals
sub: Values, types, operators, strings, arrays, objects and JSON, with the traps that catch Python programmers
goals: Run JavaScript in a jsrun box, the browser console and Node.js in Terminal
Predict how JavaScript stores numbers, compares values with == and ===, and decides truthiness
Declare variables with let and const and explain block scope, hoisting and the temporal dead zone
Process strings, arrays and objects with built-in methods chained into pipelines
Convert data to and from JSON and say what does not survive the trip

blocks.text: JavaScript is the one language every browser runs, and with Node.js it runs on servers and in your Terminal too. In this chapter you will learn its core: how values and types work (including the ones that surprise Python programmers), how to declare variables safely, how operators convert between types, and how to shape strings, arrays, objects and JSON with built-in methods chained like a shell pipeline. You already program in Python, so the chapter moves quickly over familiar ideas and slows down wherever JavaScript behaves differently. The data is the book's home LAN: the router at 192.168.1.1, the Raspberry Pi at .50, the NAS at .60 that is always offline.

Each `jsrun` block is editable and has a Run button. It runs as an ES module in a sandboxed frame, and the output is formatted exactly the way Node.js prints it, so what you see here is what `node` prints in Terminal. Predict the output before you press Run, then change one thing and run it again.
Where JavaScript runs

The language is defined by **ECMAScript** (the standard ECMA-262), maintained by a committee called TC39 that publishes a new edition every June. ES2015 (also called ES6) was the big modernization: `let` and `const`, arrow functions, classes, modules, promises, template literals. Every edition since has added a handful of features, such as `?.` and `??` (ES2020) and `toSorted()` (ES2023).
An **engine** parses the source, starts running it in an interpreter and compiles frequently run functions to machine code with a JIT (just-in-time) compiler:

`console.log` prints its arguments separated by spaces, formatting non-strings the way the REPL does. `console.error` and `console.warn` print the same way but, in Node, write to **stderr** (file descriptor 2, from [Pipes](#pipes)); a browser shows them red or yellow.

Syntax: statements, semicolons and comments

A program is a list of **statements** (declarations, `if`, loops, `return`), and statements contain **expressions** (anything that produces a value: `2 + 3`, `f(x)`, `a ? b : c`). Curly braces group statements into a **block**. Unlike Python, indentation and line breaks mean nothing to the parser; formatting is a matter of style, usually enforced by a formatter such as Prettier.

items.text: **Identifiers** may contain letters, digits, `_` and `$`, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive (`hostName` and `hostname` are different). The conventions are `camelCase` for variables and functions, `PascalCase` for classes and `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` for fixed configuration values.
**Comments** are `//` to the end of the line and `/* ... */` for a block.

**Semicolons** end statements. If you omit one, the parser applies **automatic semicolon insertion** (ASI): when a line break comes before a token that cannot continue the current statement, it inserts the semicolon for you.

blocks.text: ASI works most of the time and fails in two specific ways. First, a line break right after `return`, `break`, `continue`, `throw` or `yield` always ends the statement. Second, a line that starts with `(`, `[`, a backtick, `+`, `-` or `/` is glued onto the previous line, because each of those tokens can continue an expression.

The first function returns `undefined`: the parser ended the statement after `return`, and the braces below became a block containing a label (`port:`) and the number 8080. In the second case the two lines became one expression, `[22, 80][443, 8443].forEach(...)`: the comma operator turns `443, 8443` into `8443`, index 8443 of a two-element array is `undefined`, and calling `.forEach` on `undefined` throws a `TypeError`. V8's message is "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'forEach')"; Safari words it differently, so in this book error examples print `error.name` rather than the message.

Both styles (always semicolons, or never semicolons plus a leading `;` before lines that start with `(` or `[`) are common. This book uses semicolons. Either way, put the opening brace of a returned object on the same line as `return`.
Strict mode

JavaScript has two dialects. **Strict mode** turns several silent mistakes into errors: assigning to an undeclared variable throws a `ReferenceError`, writing to a read-only property throws a `TypeError`, `this` in a plain function call is `undefined`, and a few legacy features (`with`, octal literals like `010`) are forbidden. ES modules and class bodies are always strict, and so is every jsrun box in this book. Old-style **classic scripts** are sloppy unless they start with `'use strict';`. This box runs as a classic script:

blocks.code:
portt = 8080;   // a typo: no let or const
console.log(typeof portt, globalThis.portt);

blocks.text: The typo silently created a global variable. In a module the same line is an error:

Browsers cannot break the billions of pages written before 2009, so sloppy mode stays the default for classic scripts forever. Strict mode was introduced in ES5 as an opt-in, and ES2015 made it the only mode for modules and classes. Write modules and you never have to think about it.
Values and types

JavaScript has seven **primitive** types and one structured type, **object**. Primitives are immutable values; objects (which include arrays, functions, dates and maps) are mutable and are reached through references, exactly like names and objects in Python.

blocks.text: Three results need explaining:

items.text: `typeof null` is `'object'`. The first implementation stored a type tag with each value, used tag 0 for objects, and represented `null` as the null pointer, whose tag was also 0. Fixing it would break old code, so it stays. Test for null with `value === null`.
Arrays report `'object'` because they are objects. Use `Array.isArray(value)`.
`typeof` on a name that was never declared returns `'undefined'` instead of throwing. Scripts use this for feature detection: `typeof window !== 'undefined'` is true only in a browser.

blocks.name: typeof
blocks.sum: Return a string naming the type of a value.

how.text: `typeof` is an operator, not a function, so the parentheses in `typeof(x)` are just grouping. It returns one of eight strings: `'number'`, `'bigint'`, `'string'`, `'boolean'`, `'undefined'`, `'symbol'`, `'function'` or `'object'`. Every object that is not callable reports `'object'`, including arrays, dates, maps and `null`.

It is the only way to touch an undeclared name without a `ReferenceError`, which makes it useful for checking whether a global API exists (except for a `let` or `const` name inside its temporal dead zone, where it throws too).

examples.desc: The eight answers
examples.code:
console.log(typeof 1, typeof 1n, typeof '', typeof false);
console.log(typeof undefined, typeof Symbol(), typeof Math.max, typeof null);
examples.out:
number bigint string boolean
undefined symbol function object

examples.desc: Count the types in a mixed array
examples.code:
const mixed = [1, 'a', null, [2], { b: 3 }, 4];
console.log(mixed.map((v) => (v === null ? 'null' : Array.isArray(v) ? 'array' : typeof v)).join(' '));

gotchas: `typeof null === 'object'` and `typeof [] === 'object'`. Use `=== null` and `Array.isArray()` for those two.

blocks.text: Numbers: one type, 64-bit floats

Every `number` is an IEEE 754 double-precision float: 64 bits, 52 of which store the significant digits (53 bits of precision, counting an implicit leading 1). There is no separate integer type, so `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and integers are exact only up to 2 to the 53rd power minus 1, which is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (9007199254740991). Above that, consecutive integers can no longer all be represented.

The same `0.30000000000000004` you saw in Python appears for the same reason: 0.1 has no exact binary form. Division by zero does not throw; it gives `Infinity` or `-Infinity`, and `0 / 0` gives `NaN` ("not a number", which is of type number). There is even a negative zero, `-0`, which compares equal to `0`. Number literals accept the same prefixes and `_` separators as Python. The parentheses in `(255).toString(16)` stop the parser from reading `255.` as a decimal point.
BigInt for integers beyond 2 to the 53rd

A **BigInt** is an arbitrary-size integer written with an `n` suffix. You need it for values such as 64-bit interface byte counters from SNMP, database IDs, or nanosecond timestamps, all of which exceed the safe range.

BigInt division truncates toward zero, and mixing BigInt with number in arithmetic throws a `TypeError` instead of silently losing precision: convert explicitly with `BigInt(n)` or `Number(big)`. The fourth line shows why it matters: the number literal 9007199254740993 cannot be stored and quietly becomes ...992. BigInt cannot be used with `Math` functions and is not supported by `JSON.stringify`.
null and undefined

JavaScript has two "no value" values. **undefined** means a slot exists but nothing was ever put in it: a declared variable without a value, a missing property, a missing argument, the result of a function without `return`. **null** is a value you assign on purpose to say "empty". APIs follow the same convention: a property that does not exist is `undefined`, while a JSON field that the server explicitly set to nothing arrives as `null`.

blocks.text: Symbols

A **symbol** is a unique value, usually used as an object key that cannot clash with any string key. Two symbols with the same description are still different. You will mostly meet the built-in ones, such as `Symbol.iterator`, which tells `for...of` how to loop over an object ([JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/iterators)).
Values and references

Assigning a primitive copies the value. Assigning an object copies the **reference**, so two names can point at one object, and `===` on objects asks "is this the same object?", never "do these look the same?".
Variables: let, const and var
Three keywords declare variables. Modern code uses two of them.

blocks.text: A **block** is any pair of braces: the body of an `if`, a loop or a bare `{ }`. A `let` or `const` declared inside exists only there. `var` ignores blocks and belongs to the enclosing function (or to the global object, in a classic script).

`const` freezes the **binding**, not the value. You cannot point the name at something else, but you can change the object it points to. `Object.freeze(obj)` makes an object's own properties read-only (one level deep).
Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
When the engine enters a scope it first registers every declaration in it; this is called **hoisting**. What a name holds before its line runs depends on the keyword:

blocks.code:
entering the scope              running line by line
  ───────────────────────────     ──────────────────────────────────────
  function f → whole function     f()            → works above its line
  var a      → undefined          console.log(a) → undefined, no error
  let b      → ⟪r:uninitialized⟫      console.log(b) → ⟪r:ReferenceError (TDZ)⟫
                                  let b = 2;     → b usable from here on

blocks.text: The stretch between the start of the scope and the `let`/`const` line is the **temporal dead zone** (TDZ). It exists so that reading a variable before it is set fails loudly instead of quietly giving `undefined`.

blocks.text: Both attempts throw a `TypeError`: writing to a frozen property ("Cannot assign to read only property 'port'") and reassigning a `const` ("Assignment to constant variable"). In sloppy mode the first one would fail silently.

blocks.name: const
blocks.sum: Declare a block-scoped name that cannot be reassigned.
blocks.syntax: const name = value;    const { a, b } = object;    const [x, y] = array;

how.text: `const` creates a binding in the nearest enclosing block and requires an initial value. Assigning to the name again throws `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.` The value itself is not protected: elements can be pushed to a `const` array and properties changed on a `const` object.
Reach for `const` first, so that `let` signals "this changes later".

blocks.name: let
blocks.sum: Declare a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned.
blocks.syntax: let name;    let name = value;    let a = 1, b = 2;

how.text: `let` creates a binding scoped to the nearest block. Without an initializer it starts as `undefined`. Declaring the same name twice in one scope is a `SyntaxError`, and reading it before its declaration line throws a `ReferenceError` (the temporal dead zone).
In a `for (let i = 0; ...)` loop every iteration gets its own copy of `i` ([JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/closures) shows why that matters).

At the top level of a classic script it becomes a property of the global object (`window.name` in a browser). In an ES module, top-level `var` stays inside the module.

blocks.text: Operators
Arithmetic

The arithmetic operators are `+ - * / %` and `**` (power, so `2 ** 10` is 1024), plus `++` and `--`. Division always produces a float. `%` is the **remainder** and takes the sign of the left operand, so `-7 % 2` is `-1` where Python's modulo gives `1`. For integer division use `Math.trunc(a / b)` (toward zero) or `Math.floor(a / b)` (toward negative infinity, like Python's floor division).

`+` is the odd one out. If either side is a string, it converts the other side to a string and concatenates, and it works left to right. Every other arithmetic operator converts its operands to numbers.

`1 + 2 + 'px'` is `'3px'` because the numbers are added before the string appears; `'px' + 1 + 2` is `'px12'`. Unary `+` converts to a number and is a common shorthand for `Number(x)`. Postfix `n++` returns the old value, prefix `++n` the new one.
Equality: === and ==

`===` (strict equality) is true only when both sides have the same type and the same value; it never converts. `==` (loose equality) first converts the operands according to a set of rules from 1995 that nobody memorises. The table shows why style guides ban it:

blocks.text: Notice that `==` is not even transitive: `0 == ''` and `0 == '0'` but `'' != '0'`. Use `===` and `!==` everywhere. The one widely accepted exception is `value == null`, which is true for both `null` and `undefined`. To compare with `NaN` use `Number.isNaN(x)`; `Object.is(a, b)` is like `===` except that `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false.

[0,""]           true false
[0,"0"]          true false
["","0"]         false false
[false,"0"]      true false
[null,null]      true false

blocks.text: `JSON.stringify` prints `undefined` and `NaN` as `null`, which is why two rows look like `[null,null]`; the comparisons themselves used the real values. The last line covers the relational operators: two strings compare by UTF-16 code unit, so `'10' < '9'` is true and uppercase sorts before lowercase, while a string against a number compares numerically.

blocks.name: === (strict equality)
blocks.sum: Compare two values without type conversion; !== is its negation.

how.text: The result is true when both operands have the same type and the same value. Primitives compare by value; objects (including arrays and functions) compare by identity, so two separately created but identical-looking objects are not equal. The two special cases are `NaN === NaN`, which is false, and `0 === -0`, which is true.
Compare objects by their contents yourself: a key such as `id`, or `JSON.stringify` for small plain data.

blocks.text: Logical operators, ?? and ?.

`&&`, `||` and `!` short-circuit and, like Python's `and` and `or`, return one of their operands rather than a boolean. `a || b` returns `a` if it is truthy, otherwise `b`, which made it the traditional way to supply defaults. The trap is that `0`, `''` and `false` are legitimate values that `||` throws away.

The **nullish coalescing** operator `??` returns its right side only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. **Optional chaining** `?.` stops and returns `undefined` when the value before it is `null` or `undefined`, instead of throwing; it has three forms: `obj?.prop`, `obj?.[key]` and `fn?.()`. The **logical assignment** operators `||=`, `&&=` and `??=` assign only when the corresponding test says so.

blocks.name: ?? (nullish coalescing)
blocks.sum: Return the right operand only when the left one is null or undefined.

how.text: `a ?? b` evaluates `a`; if it is anything other than `null` or `undefined`, that is the result and `b` is never evaluated. Unlike `||`, it keeps the falsy-but-valid values `0`, `''`, `false` and `NaN`, which makes it the right operator for defaults of numbers, strings and flags.
`a ??= b` assigns only when `a` is nullish, filling in a missing setting without touching one set to 0.

const load1 = (await res.json()).load?.[0] ?? 0;

gotchas: `a || b ?? c` is a SyntaxError. Add parentheses to say which you mean.

blocks.name: ?. (optional chaining)
blocks.sum: Access a property, index or call only if the value before it is not null or undefined.

how.text: If the left side is `null` or `undefined`, the whole chain from that point **short-circuits** to `undefined`: nothing to the right is evaluated, including function calls in the arguments. Otherwise it behaves like `.`, `[]` or `()`.

Use it where a value may legitimately be missing (optional API fields, DOM elements that might not exist). When a value must exist, a loud `TypeError` is more useful than an `undefined` that fails somewhere else later.

gotchas: `?.` protects only against `null` and `undefined`. `dev.name?.foo.bar` still throws if `foo` is missing, because the second `.` is unprotected.

blocks.text: Spread and rest

Three dots do two opposite jobs. As **spread**, `...` unpacks an iterable or object into a surrounding array literal, object literal or argument list. As **rest**, in a parameter list or destructuring pattern, it collects the remaining items into a new array or object.
Later properties win, so `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }` is the idiom for merging configuration. Spreading copies only one level deep: nested objects are shared, not duplicated.

blocks.name: ... (spread and rest)
blocks.sum: Expand an iterable or object in place (spread), or gather the remaining items (rest).

how.text: In an array literal or call, spread iterates its operand (arrays, strings, Sets, Maps, NodeLists) and inserts each item. In an object literal it copies the source's own enumerable properties; when two sources share a key, the later one wins.
As a rest parameter, `...name` must be last and receives the extra arguments as a real array (Python's `*args`).

examples.desc: Copy, merge and gather
De-duplicate, sort and join in one expression
examples.code: const unique = [...new Set(['pi', 'nas', 'pi', 'router'])].toSorted().join(' ');

gotchas: Spread copies are shallow. Changing `copy.net.vlan` also changes `original.net.vlan`; use `structuredClone()` for a deep copy.

blocks.text: Bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers

`& | ^ ~ << >>` convert their operands to **32-bit signed integers**, operate on the bits and convert back. That matters for IPv4, which is exactly 32 bits: shifting 192 left by 24 sets the sign bit and gives a negative number. The unsigned right shift `>>>` reinterprets the result as unsigned, and `>>> 0` is the idiom for "treat these 32 bits as an unsigned number".

The address came out as -1062731390 until `>>> 0` turned it into 3232235906, the same integer Python's `int(ipaddress.ip_address(...))` gives. Network and broadcast addresses come out right because the bit patterns are right; only the sign interpretation differed.

The shift count is taken modulo 32, so `0xffffffff << 32` shifts by 0 and leaves all bits set. A `/0` mask computed as `0xffffffff << (32 - prefix)` is therefore wrong; handle prefix 0 separately or build masks with arithmetic (`2 ** 32 - 2 ** (32 - prefix)`).
Truthiness

Conditions (`if`, `while`, `? :`, `&&`, `||`, `!`) convert their value to a boolean. Exactly eight values are **falsy**: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Every other value is **truthy**, including the string `'0'`, the string `'false'` and, unlike Python, every array and every object, even empty ones.

`filter(Boolean)` passes each value to the `Boolean` function, which returns its truthiness, so it keeps exactly the truthy ones. Because empty arrays are truthy, say what you mean when testing collections: `if (list.length > 0)`, `if (Object.keys(obj).length)`, `if (value != null)`.

`if (device.port)` skips port 0, `if (count)` skips a count of zero, and `const retries = opts.retries || 3` turns an explicit 0 into 3. When 0 or an empty string is meaningful, test `=== undefined` or use `??`.
Strings

Strings are written with single quotes, double quotes (identical) or backticks. A backtick string is a **template literal**: it can span lines, and `${expression}` inside it inserts the value of any expression, like an f-string. Escapes are the familiar `\n`, `\t`, `\\` and `\'`, plus `\u{1D11E}` for any Unicode code point.

next free port: 8081, ssh: yes
host: pi
ip:   192.168.1.50

blocks.text: `String.raw` is a built-in **tag**: a function placed in front of a template literal that receives the raw pieces, here leaving backslashes alone (the equivalent of Python's `r"..."`).

blocks.name: Template literal
blocks.sum: A backtick string that can span lines and interpolate expressions with ${...}.

how.text: Each `${...}` is evaluated, converted to a string with `String()` and spliced in. Any expression works: arithmetic, method calls, ternaries, even another template literal. Line breaks inside the backticks are kept literally, which makes multi-line text easy (indentation is kept too, so mind it).
A **tagged** template calls a function with the literal pieces and the values separately; libraries use tags for HTML escaping and SQL parameters.

Build one line per device and join them

blocks.text: Strings are UTF-16 and immutable

A JavaScript string is a sequence of 16-bit **UTF-16 code units**, and `.length` counts code units, not characters. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (many symbols, rare CJK characters, emoji) take two code units, a **surrogate pair**. Spreading a string or looping over it with `for...of` walks by code point instead. Accented letters can also be stored two ways: as one precomposed code point, or as a base letter plus a combining mark; `normalize('NFC')` converts to the precomposed form so that comparisons work.

`TextEncoder` converts a string to UTF-8 bytes, the same job as Python's `.encode()`: "café" is 4 code units but 5 bytes. When you count characters for display, use `[...s].length`; when you size a network payload, count bytes.
Strings cannot be changed in place. Every method returns a new string, and assigning to an index is ignored in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode:

blocks.name: String.prototype.split()
blocks.sum: Cut a string into an array of substrings at every occurrence of a separator.

how.text: The separator can be a string or a regular expression. Every occurrence splits, so two separators in a row produce an empty string, and a separator at the start or end produces an empty first or last item. `split('')` splits into UTF-16 code units (use `[...str]` for characters). The optional `limit` caps the number of items returned; the rest of the string is discarded, unlike Python's `maxsplit`, which keeps it.

blocks.name: String.prototype.trim()
blocks.sum: Return a copy without whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines, other Unicode spaces) at both ends.

how.text: Removes whitespace and line terminators from the start and end only; inner whitespace stays. `trimStart` and `trimEnd` do one side. Text read from files, forms and other programs' output usually ends in `\n`, so trimming before comparing or converting is a reflex worth building.

blocks.name: String.prototype.padStart()
blocks.sum: Pad the start (or with padEnd, the end) of a string to a target length.

how.text: If the string is shorter than `targetLength`, the pad string is repeated (and cut) on the left until the length matches; `padEnd` pads on the right. A string already at or over the target length is returned unchanged, never truncated. Numbers must be converted first (`String(n)` or a template literal).
They replace Python's format specs `:>8` and `:<8`; `padStart(n, '0')` zero-pads.

blocks.name: String.prototype.replaceAll()
blocks.sum: Return a copy with every occurrence of a substring replaced (replace changes only the first).

how.text: With a string `search`, `replace` changes only the **first** occurrence, a classic surprise for Python programmers, whose `str.replace` changes all. `replaceAll` changes every occurrence. Both return new strings.
Both also accept a regular expression ([JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/regex)). In the replacement string `$&` means "the matched text", so write `$$` for a literal dollar sign.

blocks.name: String.prototype.slice()
blocks.sum: Extract the part of a string from start up to (not including) end; negative positions count from the end.

how.text: The JavaScript spelling of Python's `s[start:end]`: `s.slice(1, 4)` is `s[1:4]` and `s.slice(-2)` is `s[-2:]`. There is no step argument. Out-of-range positions are clamped instead of throwing. The older `substring` treats negative numbers as 0 and swaps its arguments when start is larger; prefer `slice`.

how.text: All three return booleans and are case-sensitive. They are clearer than `indexOf(s) !== -1`, which is what code written before 2015 uses. For case-insensitive tests, lower-case both sides first; for patterns, use a regular expression's `test`.

blocks.text: Numbers, conversion and Math
Text arrives as strings from everywhere (forms, URLs, files, `split()`), so converting to numbers is constant work. JavaScript gives you two converters with different rules:

items.text: **`Number(x)`** converts the whole value or gives `NaN`. It ignores surrounding whitespace, understands `0x`, `0b`, `0o` and exponents, and has traps: `Number('')` and `Number('   ')` are 0, and `Number(null)` is 0 while `Number(undefined)` is `NaN`.

**`parseInt(text, radix)`** reads leading digits in the given base and stops at the first character that does not fit, so `parseInt('22/tcp', 10)` is 22 and `parseInt('1e3', 10)` is 1. It returns `NaN` only when no digit was read. `parseFloat` does the same for decimals.

blocks.text: **NaN** is what failed numeric operations produce. It is the only value not equal to itself, so `x === NaN` is always false. `Number.isNaN(x)` tests for it exactly; the older global `isNaN(x)` converts first, so `isNaN('abc')` is true even though `'abc'` is a string.

blocks.out:
42 NaN 0 42 31 0 NaN
22 255 192 1 3.14
false true true false true
1.00 2.3 0.30 string
3 -2 -3 -2 -2
48 -Infinity Infinity 5

blocks.text: `toFixed` returns a **string** and rounds the stored binary value, which is why `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `'1.00'`: 1.005 is really 1.00499999999999989... `Math.round` rounds halves toward positive infinity (`Math.round(-2.5)` is -2), unlike Python's banker's rounding. `Math.max()` with no arguments returns `-Infinity`, the identity value for "largest so far".
The best-known conversion trap combines `parseInt` with `map`:

`map` calls its callback with three arguments: the value, the index and the array. `parseInt` accepts a second argument, the radix, so it received `('80', 1)`, `('443', 2)` and `('8080', 3)`: base 1 is invalid, and 4 and 8 are not digits in base 2 or 3. `Number` takes only one argument, so `map(Number)` is safe.

For display, `toLocaleString` and the `Intl.NumberFormat` API format numbers with thousands separators, units and percentages. Always pass the locale explicitly in code whose output you test, because the default is the user's.

blocks.name: Number()
blocks.sum: Convert any value to a number, strictly: the whole string must be numeric or the result is NaN.

how.text: Strings are trimmed, then parsed as decimal, `0x`/`0o`/`0b` integers, exponent notation or `Infinity`; anything else gives `NaN`. Booleans give 1 or 0, `null` gives 0, `undefined` gives `NaN`, and objects are first converted to a primitive (`[5]` becomes `'5'`, then 5).
Unary `+x` performs the same conversion. Never call it with `new`, which creates a wrapper object.

examples.desc: Strict conversion and its traps
examples.code: console.log(Number('8080'), Number('8080/tcp'), Number(''), Number(true), Number([5]), Number('1_000'));

blocks.name: parseInt()
blocks.sum: Parse the leading integer of a string in a given base, ignoring anything after it.

how.text: Leading whitespace and an optional sign are skipped, then digits valid in `radix` (2 to 36) are read until the first invalid character. If no digit was read the result is `NaN`. Without a radix, a `0x` prefix switches to base 16; always pass 10 (or the base you mean) to avoid guessing. `parseFloat(string)` is the decimal equivalent and has no radix.

examples.desc: Bases and trailing junk
examples.code: console.log(parseInt('ff', 16), parseInt('11000000', 2), parseInt('0x1F'), parseInt('22/tcp', 10), parseInt('px10', 10));

gotchas: `arr.map(parseInt)` passes the index as the radix and returns `[22, NaN, NaN, ...]`. Write `arr.map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))` or `arr.map(Number)`.

blocks.name: Number.isNaN()
blocks.sum: Return true only if the value is the number NaN, without converting it first.

how.text: `NaN !== NaN`, so equality cannot detect it. `Number.isNaN` checks for the actual NaN value. The global `isNaN` converts its argument to a number first, so it reports true for any string that is not numeric, which makes it a vague "is this not a number?" test. Related checks: `Number.isInteger`, `Number.isSafeInteger` and `Number.isFinite`, none of which convert.

examples.desc: Detect a failed conversion
examples.code:
const port = Number('ssh');
console.log(port === NaN, Number.isNaN(port), isNaN('ssh'), Number.isNaN('ssh'));

examples.desc: Keep only the fields that converted cleanly
examples.code: const nums = ['22', 'x', '443'].map(Number).filter((n) => !Number.isNaN(n));

blocks.name: Number.prototype.toFixed()
blocks.sum: Format a number with a fixed count of decimals, returning a string.

how.text: Rounds the stored binary value to `digits` places (0 to 100) and returns text, so the result cannot be used for further arithmetic without converting back. Because the binary value is used, halfway cases can round down (`(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `'1.00'`). Related: `toPrecision(n)` for significant digits, `toString(radix)` for other bases, `Intl.NumberFormat` for separators and units.

examples.code:

console.log(rtt.toFixed(2), rtt.toFixed(0), (0.5).toFixed(0), typeof rtt.toFixed(1));

console.log(`${avg.toFixed(1)} ms`);

gotchas: `(2.5).toFixed(0) + 1` is `'31'`, because `toFixed` returned a string. Do the arithmetic first, format last.

blocks.name: Math.round()
blocks.sum: Round to the nearest integer, halves toward positive infinity; Math.floor, ceil and trunc round in fixed directions.

how.text: `Math` is a plain object holding constants (`Math.PI`) and functions; it is not a constructor. `round` sends .5 upward, so 2.5 becomes 3 and -2.5 becomes -2. `floor` goes down, `ceil` goes up, `trunc` drops the fraction (toward zero). To round to two places, scale: `Math.round(x * 100) / 100`, or format with `toFixed`.
`Math.random()` is not suitable for security tokens; use `crypto.getRandomValues()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`.

examples.code: for (const x of [2.5, -2.5, 2.4]) console.log(x, Math.round(x), Math.floor(x), Math.ceil(x), Math.trunc(x));

blocks.text: Control flow

`if`/`else` works as you expect, with the condition in parentheses and the body in braces. The **conditional operator** `cond ? a : b` is an expression (Python's `a if cond else b`). `switch` compares with `===` and falls through until `break` (see its card).
Loops:

items.text: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` is the C-style counting loop.

`for (const x of iterable)` walks the **values** of anything iterable: arrays, strings (by code point), Maps, Sets, NodeLists. This is Python's `for x in xs`. Use `arr.entries()` to get `[index, value]` pairs, like `enumerate`.
`for (const key in object)` walks the enumerable **string keys** of an object, including inherited ones. On arrays it yields indices as strings plus any extra properties, so do not use it on arrays.
`while (cond)` and `do { } while (cond)`; the second always runs at least once.
`break` leaves a loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration, and a **label** (`outer:`) lets `break outer` leave a nested loop in one step.

blocks.text: `for...in` on the array produced the string keys `'0'`, `'1'` and the stray `'note'`; `for...of` produced the numbers. On a plain object `for...in` is fine, though `Object.entries` (below) is usually clearer.

blocks.name: for...of
blocks.sum: Loop over the values of any iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists, generators.

how.text: `for...of` asks the object for an iterator (its `Symbol.iterator` method) and calls `next()` until it reports done. Each iteration gets a fresh binding, so `const` works. `break`, `continue` and `return` behave normally, which is the main advantage over `forEach`, where `break` is impossible.
Destructure pairs in the header: `arr.entries()`, `Object.entries(obj)` or a Map. Plain objects are not iterable; looping over one throws `TypeError: obj is not iterable`.

Stop at the first offline device, which forEach cannot do

blocks.name: for...in
blocks.sum: Loop over the enumerable string keys of an object, including inherited ones.

how.text: Keys come in the standard order (integer-like keys ascending, then other strings in insertion order), and enumerable inherited keys are included. Read values with `object[key]`. Use it, if at all, on plain data objects, never on arrays.

examples.desc: Keys of an object
examples.code:

for (const k in counts) console.log(k, counts[k]);

examples.code: const busy = Object.entries({ 200: 57, 404: 11 }).filter(([, n]) => n > 20).map(([code]) => code);

gotchas: `for (const i in [10, 20])` gives `'0'` and `'1'` as strings, so `i + 1` is `'01'`.

blocks.name: switch
blocks.sum: Jump to the case whose value is strictly equal (===) to an expression and run until break.

how.text: The expression is evaluated once and compared with each `case` value using `===`, top to bottom. Execution starts at the first match and **falls through** into the following cases until a `break`, `return` or `throw`. `default` runs when nothing matches. Stacking `case a: case b:` with no code between them shares one body. Each `case` does not get its own block scope unless you add braces.
For mapping a value to a result, an object lookup (`const kind = { router: 'network', server: 'host' }[type] ?? 'other'`) is often shorter.

examples.desc: Fall-through used on purpose
Count requests per status class with the same function
examples.code: const classes = [200, 404, 200, 503].map(kindOf).reduce((acc, k) => ({ ...acc, [k]: (acc[k] ?? 0) + 1 }), {});

gotchas: `switch ('1') { case 1: ... }` never matches, because the comparison is `===` and a string is not a number.

blocks.text: Functions

There are three ways to create a function. A **declaration** is hoisted (callable above its line). An **expression** assigns a function to a variable. An **arrow function** is the compact form used for callbacks; with no braces after the arrow, its body is a single expression whose value is returned.

blocks.code:
function area(w, h) { return w * h; }              // declaration, hoisted
const area2 = function (w, h) { return w * h; };   // function expression
const area3 = (w, h) => w * h;                     // arrow function, implicit return
const square = (x) => x * x;                       // one parameter
const makeDevice = (name) => ({ name, online: true }); // parentheses around an object result

blocks.text: The calling rules differ from Python in ways that cause quiet bugs:

items.text: Missing arguments are `undefined`, and extra arguments are ignored. Nothing throws `TypeError: missing argument`.

A **default parameter** (`port = 22`) applies when the argument is missing or explicitly `undefined`, not when it is `null`. Defaults are evaluated on every call, so `list = []` gives a fresh array each time; Python's mutable-default trap does not exist.
A **rest parameter** `...args` collects the extra arguments into a real array (Python's `*args`).
There are no keyword arguments. Pass an object and destructure it in the parameter list ([JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/modern) shows the pattern).
`return` without a value, or reaching the end, returns `undefined`.

blocks.text: `noParens` returns `undefined`: without parentheses the braces are a function body containing the expression `online`, not an object. `connect.length` is 1 because a function's `length` counts the parameters before the first default or rest parameter.

Functions are values: you pass them to other functions (**callbacks**), return them and store them. Every array method in the next section takes a callback. Arrow functions also treat `this` differently, which [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/this) explains.

blocks.name: function
blocks.sum: Declare a named, hoisted function.
blocks.syntax: function name(param1, param2 = default, ...rest) { ... return value; }

how.text: A function declaration creates a binding for `name` in the enclosing scope and initializes it with the whole function before any code in that scope runs, so it can be called above its definition. Parameters behave like `let` variables local to the call. The function's `name` property is the declared name, which stack traces show.
Functions are objects: they can be passed, returned and given properties.

blocks.name: => (arrow function)
blocks.sum: A compact function expression; with an expression body, its value is returned implicitly.
blocks.syntax: (a, b) => expression    (a) => { statements; return value; }    () => ({ key: value })

how.text: Parentheses around a single parameter are optional. With braces the body is a normal block and needs `return`; without braces it is a single expression that is returned. To return an object literal, wrap it in parentheses so the braces are not read as a block.

Arrow functions have no `this`, `arguments` or `prototype` of their own and cannot be called with `new`. They take `this` from the surrounding code, which makes them ideal for callbacks inside methods and unsuitable as methods themselves.

blocks.text: Arrays

An array is an ordered list of values of any type, written `[a, b, c]`. Its `length` is one more than the highest index. Reading past the end gives `undefined` (there is no `IndexError`), `arr.at(-1)` reads from the end, and setting `length` shorter truncates the array. Arrays are objects, so `typeof` says `'object'`; use `Array.isArray`.
Array methods fall into two families, and mixing them up causes real bugs:

head: Changes the array in place
Returns something new, leaves the array alone

blocks.text: Sorting needs a comparator

`sort()` without arguments compares elements as strings: right for lowercase names, wrong for numbers, mixed case and IP addresses. A **comparator** `(a, b) =>` returns a negative number to put `a` first, a positive number to put `b` first, 0 to keep their order: `a - b` sorts numbers ascending, `b - a` descending, `a.localeCompare(b)` sorts text the way people expect. Both `sort` (in place) and `toSorted` (a copy) are stable, so sorting by a secondary key and then by the primary key gives a correct two-level order.
`ipKey` uses multiplication instead of `<<` so the result stays a positive number (the bitwise version would need `>>> 0`, as shown in the operators section).
Flattening, building and destructuring arrays

`Array.from({ length: 4 }, fn)` generates elements from an empty array-like, the usual stand-in for Python's `range`. **Array destructuring** unpacks by position, and `[a, b] = [b, a]` swaps two variables. The semicolon ending the `let` line matters: without it, ASI would glue `[a, b]` onto that line.

blocks.text: Objects

An object is a collection of **properties**: string (or symbol) keys with values. Quotes around keys are optional when the key is a valid identifier and required otherwise (`'content-type'`). Read properties with a dot when the key is a fixed identifier, and with brackets when it contains other characters or is held in a variable.

Object literals have three shorthands: `{ host, port }` means `{ host: host, port: port }`, `describe() { ... }` defines a method, and `[expr]: value` computes the key. A missing property reads as `undefined`, never a `KeyError`. To test whether a key exists, `'ip' in obj` also sees inherited keys, while `Object.hasOwn(obj, 'ip')` checks only the object's own properties. `delete obj.key` removes a property.

blocks.text: `'toString' in d` is true because every plain object inherits `toString` from `Object.prototype` (the prototype chain is the subject of [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/prototypes)). Inside `describe`, `this` is the object the method was called on.
Keys are strings, and their order has a rule

Property keys are always strings or symbols. A number used as a key is converted to a string, so `obj[1]` and `obj['1']` are the same property, and an object used as a key becomes the string `'[object Object]'`. Key order follows a fixed rule: **integer-like keys first, in ascending numeric order**, then the other string keys in insertion order, then symbols. Ports and status codes used as keys therefore come out sorted, whatever order you inserted them in. When you need arbitrary key types or strict insertion order, use a `Map` ([JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/map-set)).
entries, fromEntries and destructuring

`Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` turn an object into arrays, so every array method becomes available; `Object.fromEntries` turns `[key, value]` pairs back into an object. **Object destructuring** pulls properties into variables by name, with renaming, defaults, nesting and a rest pattern.

The `[, ms]` pattern skips the first element of each pair. The final line is the shallow-copy trap: `merged` got its own `ip`, but `merged.net` and `device.net` are one object, so changing the VLAN through one name changed it for both. `structuredClone(device)` makes a true deep copy.

blocks.name: Destructuring assignment
blocks.sum: Unpack array items by position or object properties by name into variables.

how.text: Array patterns use the iterator, so they work on any iterable; holes (`[, second]`) skip items. Object patterns read properties by name; `key: alias` renames, `= value` supplies a default used only for `undefined`, and patterns nest to any depth. Destructuring a property of `undefined` or `null` throws a `TypeError`, so give nested patterns a default object (`{ net: { gw } = {} }`) when the branch may be missing. The same patterns work in parameter lists and `for...of` headers.

blocks.text: JSON

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation, RFC 8259) is the text format of nearly every web API. Its syntax was taken from JavaScript literals but is stricter: keys and strings need double quotes, trailing commas and comments are forbidden, and the only values are objects, arrays, strings, numbers, `true`, `false` and `null`. There is no `undefined`, no function, no `NaN` or `Infinity`, no BigInt and no date type (dates travel as ISO 8601 strings by convention).

`JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)` turns a value into JSON text, and `JSON.parse(text, reviver)` turns text back into values. Everything JSON cannot represent is dropped or converted silently, which is worth seeing once:

Read the first line closely: the date became a string (through its `toJSON` method), `NaN` and `Infinity` became `null`, the `undefined` property and the method vanished, and the Set became an empty object because it has no enumerable properties. Parsing gives the date back as a plain string; a **reviver** function, called for every key and value, can turn it into a `Date` again. Single quotes and trailing commas are syntax errors, and BigInt throws a `TypeError`.
Every `fetch` that sends JSON uses `JSON.stringify` for the body, and `response.json()` is `JSON.parse` applied to the response body; [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper/fetch) builds on both.

blocks.name: JSON.stringify()
blocks.sum: Convert a value to a JSON string, optionally filtering keys and pretty-printing.

how.text: Objects become `{...}` with their own enumerable string keys, arrays become `[...]`, strings get double quotes and escapes. Properties whose value is `undefined`, a function or a symbol are omitted; in arrays those values become `null`, as do `NaN` and `Infinity`. An object with a `toJSON()` method (such as `Date`) is replaced by that method's result. BigInt values and circular references throw `TypeError`.

`replacer` is either an array of keys to keep or a function `(key, value) => newValue` called for every property (return `undefined` to drop it). `space` (a number up to 10, or a string) indents the output for humans.

how.text: The text must be valid JSON; anything else (single quotes, trailing commas, comments, `undefined`) throws a `SyntaxError`, so wrap parsing of untrusted input in `try/catch`. The result is plain objects and arrays: dates stay strings and numbers above 2 to the 53rd lose precision. The optional `reviver(key, value)` replaces each value with its return value, which is where ISO strings become `Date` objects again.

blocks.text: Dates and Intl, briefly
A `Date` holds a single number: milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, the Unix epoch (Python's `time.time()` counts seconds). Everything else is interpretation. The traps:

items.text: **Months count from 0**: `new Date(2026, 9, 5)` is 5 October. Days of the month count from 1.

**Parsing depends on the string.** An ISO string ending in `Z` or an offset is unambiguous. A date-only ISO string (`'2026-10-05'`) is read as UTC midnight, but a date-time without an offset (`'2026-10-05T10:00'`) is read as **local** time. Other formats are implementation-defined; do not rely on them.
`getHours()` and friends use the machine's time zone; `getUTCHours()` and `toISOString()` use UTC. Logs and APIs should use UTC.
Subtracting two dates gives milliseconds.

blocks.text: `getUTCMonth()` is 9 for October and `getUTCDay()` is 1 for Monday (Sunday is 0). The `Intl` formatters handle time zones and languages correctly, which is far safer than building date strings by hand.

`Date` has well-known design flaws, and its replacement, the `Temporal` API (separate types for instants, wall-clock times and time zones, months counted from 1), is shipping: Firefox 139 (2025), Chrome and Edge 144 (2026) and Node.js 26 have it, while Safari has it only in Safari Technology Preview as of Safari 27.2 (November 2026). Until it reaches a stable Safari, `Date` plus `Intl` is what runs everywhere; MDN's compatibility table shows the current state.

blocks.name: new Date()
blocks.sum: Create a date-time object from now, a timestamp, an ISO string or date parts.
blocks.syntax: new Date()    new Date(ms)    new Date(isoString)    new Date(year, monthIndex, day, h, m, s)    Date.now()

how.text: Internally a `Date` is milliseconds since the Unix epoch in UTC. `new Date()` is now, `Date.now()` returns now as a number. With parts, months are 0-based and the parts are local time; `Date.UTC(...)` takes the same parts as UTC and returns milliseconds. `toISOString()` always prints UTC with a `Z`, and `JSON.stringify` uses it. Dates are mutable (`setUTCHours` changes the object), so copy before changing: `new Date(d)`.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Using `==`.** It converts types with rules that are not even transitive. Use `===` and `!==`, and convert input explicitly with `Number()`.
**Sorting numbers with plain `sort()`.** It sorts as text: `[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
**`arr.map(parseInt)`.** The index becomes the radix. Use `map(Number)` or a wrapper.
**Defaults with `||`.** `port || 22` replaces a real 0; `name || 'guest'` replaces a real empty string. Use `??`.
**Testing an array for emptiness with `if (arr)`.** Empty arrays and objects are truthy. Test `arr.length`.
**`return` on its own line.** ASI returns `undefined`. Keep the value on the same line.
**Forgetting that `replace` with a string changes only the first match.** Use `replaceAll`.
**Mutating when you meant to copy.** `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` change the array; spread copies are shallow. Use `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `structuredClone`.
**Comparing objects with `===`.** It compares identity. Compare an `id`, or the JSON of small plain objects.
**Trusting `toFixed` and floats for money.** `toFixed` returns a string and rounds the binary value. Count cents in integers or use BigInt.
**Month 10 is November.** `new Date(2026, 10, 5)` is 5 November; months are 0-based.
**Expecting JSON to keep types.** Dates become strings, Maps and Sets become `{}`, `undefined` disappears.

echo 'console.log(process.argv.slice(2).map(Number).toSorted((a, b) => a - b))' > ports.js
node ports.js 8080 22 443

why.text: `process.argv` is Node's `sys.argv`. Everything on the command line arrives as text, so the conversion with `Number` is required, and without the comparator `sort` would order the numbers as strings. `console.log` printed the array in the same format the jsrun boxes use.

blocks.title: Parse a CSV string into objects

task.text: Write `parseCsv(text)` that turns CSV text with a header row into an array of objects, one per data row, using the header names as keys. Trim spaces around every field and skip blank lines. Values stay strings. Then print the names of the hosts in `csv`, separated by single spaces: `router macbook pi`.

hints: Split the text into lines with `split('\n')`, trim each line and drop empty ones with `filter`.

The first line gives the keys: `const keys = lines[0].split(',').map((k) => k.trim())`. For each other line, build pairs with `keys.map((k, i) => [k, fields[i]])` and turn them into an object with `Object.fromEntries`.

why.text: This is the same split, trim, filter, map pipeline you would write in Python, with `Object.fromEntries` playing the role of `dict(zip(keys, fields))`. Real CSV can contain quoted fields with commas inside; for that, use a library (or Python's `csv` module), because a plain `split(',')` cannot handle it.

blocks.title: Group devices by type with reduce

task.text: Write `groupByType(devices)` that returns an object mapping each device type to an array of device **names**, in the order the devices appear. Then fetch `/api/devices` from the practice server and print `JSON.stringify(groupByType(devices))`. The expected output starts with `{"router":["router"],"laptop":["macbook"],"server":["pi","homeassistant"]`.

hints: Start the accumulator as `{}`. For each device, make sure `acc[d.type]` is an array (`acc[d.type] ??= []`), then push the name.
The callback must `return acc` at the end, or the next iteration receives `undefined`.

why.text: `??=` creates the array the first time a type appears, and returning the accumulator threads it through every call. Newer runtimes (Node 21+, Chrome 117+, Safari 17.4+) have this built in: `Object.groupBy(devices, (d) => d.type)` returns arrays of whole devices in an object with no prototype, and `Map.groupBy` returns a Map.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: two silent bugs

task.text: This settings validator and port sorter run without errors and give wrong answers. Run it, read the output, then fix both functions:

items.text: `missing(obj)` must return the keys whose value is an empty string, `null` or `undefined`. A value of `0` is a real value. For the settings below it should print `[]`.
`sortedPorts(list)` must return a new array sorted numerically ascending, **without changing** the array it was given. It should print `[ 22, 80, 443, 8080 ]`.

hints: Run the starter first. What does `0 == ''` evaluate to? And what does `null == ''`?
For the sort, two things are wrong: the default order is text order, and `sort` changes the original. `toSorted` with a comparator fixes both.

why.text: `0 == ''` is true because the empty string converts to 0, while `null == ''` and `undefined == ''` are false, so the loose test was wrong in both directions. Spelling out the three cases with `===` (or `obj[k] === '' || obj[k] == null`, the one accepted use of `==`) states the rule exactly. The default `sort` compared `'22'`, `'443'`, `'80'`, `'8080'` as text and reordered the caller's array; `toSorted` with `(a, b) => a - b` returns a numeric copy.

blocks.title: Format a port table with padStart

task.text: Write `formatTable(rows)` where each row is `{ port, proto, service }`. Return one string with one line per row, sorted by port ascending (do not reorder the input array). Each line is: the port right-aligned in 5 characters, one space, the protocol left-aligned in 4 characters, one space, the service name. Lines are joined with `\n`, with no trailing newline. Print the table for `rows`. The first line is `   22 tcp  ssh`.

hints: `String(r.port).padStart(5)` and `r.proto.padEnd(4)` produce the two fixed-width columns.
Sort a copy with `rows.toSorted((a, b) => a.port - b.port)`, `map` each row to its line, then `join('\n')`.

why.text: `padStart` and `padEnd` do the job of Python's `:>5` and `:<4` format specs. Building the lines with `map` and joining at the end avoids a trailing newline, and an empty array naturally produces an empty string. `toSorted` keeps the caller's array in its original order.

task.text: Without running anything, write down the value of each expression. Then check your answers in a jsrun box or the Node REPL.

task.code:
'5' + 3 - 2
'5' - 3 + 2
true + true
[] + {}
typeof NaN
null + 1
undefined + 1
[10, 1, 2].sort()

why.text: Work left to right and remember that only `+` prefers strings. `'5' + 3` is `'53'`, then `'53' - 2` converts back to a number: 51. `'5' - 3` is 2, plus 2 is 4. Booleans convert to 1 and 0. `[] + {}` converts both objects to strings (`''` and `'[object Object]'`) and concatenates. NaN is a number value. `null` converts to 0 and `undefined` to NaN. The default sort compares `'10'`, `'1'`, `'2'` as text. If you got all eight, the coercion rules have stuck; if not, the table in the operators section is the one to reread.

questions.why: A bug from the first implementation, kept for compatibility. Test for null with `value === null`.

options.text: A TypeError, because sort needs a comparator

questions.why: Without a comparator, elements are compared as strings, and `'10'` sorts before `'9'`. Use `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.

questions.q: `const port = config.port ?? 8080` with `config.port` set to 0. What is `port`?
questions.why: `??` falls back only for `null` and `undefined`, so the configured 0 is kept. `||` would have given 8080.

questions.q: Which value is truthy in JavaScript but falsy in Python?
questions.why: Every object, including `[]` and `{}`, is truthy in JavaScript. Test `arr.length` instead.

questions.q: What does `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: [undefined, NaN] })` produce?
questions.why: Properties with `undefined` values are omitted; inside arrays, `undefined` and `NaN` become `null` so positions are kept.

questions.q: A `let` variable is read on a line above its declaration in the same block. What happens?

options.text: A ReferenceError is thrown (temporal dead zone)
It reads the global variable of the same name
A SyntaxError stops the whole script before it runs

questions.why: `let` and `const` are hoisted but stay uninitialized until their line runs. Only `var` reads as `undefined` early.
